units.intro: Grammar: the past tenses (simple, continuous, perfect) and how they work together in sentences with when, while, before and after.

cards.title: Past tenses (review)
rule: **Past simple** (verb + -ed or irregular form) = a finished action at a past time: *She **won** the race in 2019.*
**Past continuous** (was/were + -ing) = an action in progress at a past moment: *At 8 pm they **were studying**.*
**Past perfect** (had + past participle) = an action that happened **before** another past action: *The film **had started** when we arrived.*

examples.text: I visited my aunt last week.
I was visit my aunt last week.
examples.fix: I visited my aunt last week.

examples.text: When I arrived, the meeting had already begun.
She has finished the work yesterday.

cards.title: Choose between past simple, past continuous and past perfect
cards.problem: Complete: "When I ____ (arrive) at the station, the train ____ (already leave), so I ____ (wait) for the next one while it ____ (rain)."

steps.text: **Step 1: Order the events.** The train left first; then I arrived; then I waited while the rain was falling.
**Step 2: Earlier past action → past perfect.** The train had already left.
**Step 3: Main completed actions → past simple.** I arrived; I waited.
**Step 4: Background action in progress → past continuous.** It was raining.
**Tip:** "already" between had and the participle is a strong signal for the past perfect.

cards.answer: When I arrived at the station, the train had already left, so I waited for the next one while it was raining.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: I ____ in Massawa for two years before my family moved to Asmara.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** There are two past events: living in Massawa and moving to Asmara.

**Step 2:** Living in Massawa came first and lasted up to the move.

**Step 3:** The earlier action takes the past perfect: had lived.

**Tip:** Find the time words first (when, while, before, after, by the time, ago), then decide which past action came first or was in progress.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: While Selam ____ dinner, the lights went out.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Two past actions: one in progress (cooking) and one short action that interrupts it (the lights went out).

**Step 2:** The longer background action takes the past continuous: was/were + -ing.

**Step 3:** "was cooking" is correct.

**Tip:** Finished time (yesterday, ago, last…) → past simple. Long action interrupted → was/were + -ing. Earlier of two past actions → had + past participle.

**Step 3:** "visited" is the past simple form.

**Tip:** Finished time (yesterday, ago, last…) → past simple. Long action interrupted → was/were + -ing. Earlier of two past actions → had + past participle.

cards.title: Step by step: a past question with "did"
cards.problem: Complete: The teacher asked Dawit, "Why ____ (not / complete) your assignment yesterday?"

steps.text: **Step 1: Find the tense.** *yesterday* → past simple.
**Step 2: Make the question.** Wh-word + **didn't** + subject + **base verb**.
**Step 3: Check the verb.** *did* already shows the past, so the verb stays in the base form: *complete* (✗ *completed*).

cards.answer: Why didn't you complete your assignment yesterday?

cards.title: Past tenses in adverbial clauses
rule: **Past continuous + past simple:** a longer action interrupted by a short one: *While she **was cooking**, the phone **rang**.*
**Past perfect + past simple:** the earlier action uses the past perfect: *After he **had finished** his homework, he **went** out.*
Use **while** with the longer (continuous) action and **when** usually with the short action.

examples.text: While we were walking home, it started to rain.
While we walked home, it was starting to rain.
examples.fix: While we were walking home, it started to rain.

examples.text: Before the teacher came, we had cleaned the class.

cards.title: Find and correct the error
cards.problem: Find and correct the error: "While we walked home, it was starting to rain."

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the rule.** **Past continuous + past simple:** a longer action interrupted by a short one: *While she **was cooking**, the phone **rang**.*
**Step 2: Test the sentence.** "While we walked home, it was starting to rain." breaks this rule.
**Step 3: Correct it.** "While we were walking home, it started to rain."
**Check:** **Past perfect + past simple:** the earlier action uses the past perfect: *After he **had finished** his homework, he **went** out.*

cards.answer: While we were walking home, it started to rain.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: While we ________ for the school bus, it suddenly started to rain heavily.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** *While* + a long action in the past → past continuous (was/were + -ing).

**Step 2:** The subject is *we* → **were**.

**Step 3:** The short action (*it started to rain*) is in the past simple.

**Tip:** Finished time (yesterday, ago, last…) → past simple. Long action interrupted → was/were + -ing. Earlier of two past actions → had + past participle.

units.title: The Internet and You
units.intro: Grammar: active and passive voice in the present, past and future simple, and when to use the passive.

cards.title: Active and passive (1)
rule: In the **active** the subject does the action: *People **use** the Internet.* In the **passive** the subject receives the action: *The Internet **is used** by people.*
**Form:** be (in the right tense) + past participle. Present: is/are + pp; past: was/were + pp; future: will be + pp.
The object of the active sentence becomes the subject of the passive; the doer can be added with **by**.

examples.text: Emails are sent every second.
The message was send yesterday.
The new café will be opened next week.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: You must clean this machine every time you use it. (Choose the correct passive form)

options.A: This machine must clean every time.
options.B: This machine must be cleaned every time.
options.C: Every time must clean this machine.
options.D: This machine must be cleaned every time it is used.
options.E: You used this machine every time.

cards.why:
**Step 1:** Identify the structure. "must clean" is a modal active.
**Step 2:** The passive of a modal is **modal + be + Past Participle**. 
**Step 3:** "This machine must be cleaned..." matches. Choice D is more complete because it also converts "you use it" to "it is used".

cards.title: Step by step: past simple passive
cards.problem: Complete: "The report ____ (submit) by the committee last night."

steps.text: **Step 1: Who does the action?** The committee submits the report. The report does not submit anything → **passive**.
**Step 2: Find the tense.** *last night* → past simple.
**Step 3: Make the passive.** was/were + past participle → singular *report* → **was submitted**.

cards.title: Uses of the passive
rule: Use the passive when the **doer is unknown** (*My phone was stolen.*), when the **receiver is more important** (*The results will be announced on Monday.*), or when the doer is **obvious** (*He was arrested.* — by the police).
Leave out *by + doer* when it adds nothing (*by someone, by people*).

examples.text: Rice is grown in many countries.
Rice is grown by people in many countries.
examples.fix: Rice is grown in many countries.

cards.title: Find and correct the error
cards.problem: Find and correct the error: "Rice is grown by people in many countries."

**Step 2: Test the sentence.** "Rice is grown by people in many countries." breaks this rule.
**Step 3: Correct it.** "Rice is grown in many countries."
**Check:** Leave out *by + doer* when it adds nothing (*by someone, by people*).

cards.q: Which sentence is the best use of the passive?

options.A: The bridge built in 1938 by workers was.
options.D: Somebody built the bridge in 1938 by somebody.

cards.why:
**Step 1:** The builders are unknown or unimportant, so the passive focuses on the bridge.

**Step 2:** Form: was + past participle (built).

**Step 3:** The other options are ungrammatical or repeat the doer.

**Tip:** Ask "who does the action?" If the doer is unknown, unimportant or obvious, the passive (be + past participle) is usually better.

**Step 1:** Scientific writing focuses on the process, not the person.

**Step 2:** The passive (was heated) is the usual choice in reports.

**Step 3:** The other sentences are informal or ungrammatical.

**Tip:** Ask "who does the action?" If the doer is unknown, unimportant or obvious, the passive (be + past participle) is usually better.

**Step 1:** The thief receives the action; the police did it.

**Step 2:** The time is finished (yesterday), so use the past simple passive.

**Step 3:** was + past participle: was caught.

**Tip:** Ask "who does the action?" If the doer is unknown, unimportant or obvious, the passive (be + past participle) is usually better.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The high school teacher ________ a beautiful traditional gift by the students on her graduation day.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** The teacher did not give the gift – she **received** it from the students (*by the students*).

**Step 2:** So we need the passive: was + past participle → **was given**.

cards.title: Parts of speech (1)
rule: A **noun** names a person, place, thing or idea (*teacher, Keren, book, freedom*). A **pronoun** replaces a noun (*he, she, it, they, him, them*). A **verb** shows an action or state (*run, is, seem*). An **adjective** describes a noun (*a **hard-working** student*).
The same word can be different parts of speech: *a **work** of art* (noun) / *They **work** hard* (verb).

**Step 2:** After the gap comes a new subject and verb (*the board selected*), so the person is the **object** → **whom**.

**Step 3:** *who* = subject (*the candidate **who** won*); *whose* = belonging.

**Tip:** Before the verb → I, he, she, we, they. After a verb or a preposition → me, him, her, us, them.

cards.title: Step by step: Punctuation (1) – full stop, question mark, comma, capital letters
body: **Step 1:** Begin every sentence and every proper noun (names of people, places, days, months, languages) with a capital letter: "On Monday Senait went to Keren."
**Step 2:** End a statement or a polite command with a full stop (.), a direct question with a question mark (?), and a strong feeling with an exclamation mark (!).
**Step 3:** Use commas to separate items in a list: "We bought bread, milk, eggs and sugar."
**Step 4:** Use a comma after an introductory word or clause: "However, …", "When the bell rang, we left."
**Step 5:** Use a comma before "and/but/so" when they join two complete sentences, and to mark off a name you speak to: "Abel, come here."

**Example:** Wrong: "my brother lives in asmara he works in a bank" → Right: "My brother lives in Asmara. He works in a bank." (capital letters for the sentence start and the place name, a full stop between two sentences).

- **E:** Incorrect capitalization ('She' should be 'she') and the question mark should be inside the quotes.

cards.title: Linking words
rule: **and** adds, **but** contrasts, **or** gives a choice; they join words or clauses inside one sentence: *I love my country **and** I want to serve it.*
**Moreover** (addition), **however** (contrast), **therefore / hence** (result) usually start a new sentence or clause and are followed by a comma: *He was tired. **However**, he kept working.*

units.title: Politeness
units.intro: Grammar: reported (indirect) speech for statements, questions, requests and commands, and punctuation marks (colon, semi-colon, brackets, hyphen, apostrophe, quotation marks).

cards.title: Reported speech
rule: When the reporting verb is past (*said, asked, told*), the tense usually moves **one step back**: am/is → was; present simple → past simple; past simple → past perfect; will → would; can → could.
Pronouns and time words change: *now → then, today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, yesterday → the day before, here → there*.
**Questions:** *asked + if/whether* (yes/no) or *asked + wh-word*, with **statement word order** and no question mark. **Requests/commands:** *asked/told + object + (not) to + verb*.

cards.title: When the tense does NOT change
body: 1. The reporting verb is in the **present** (*says, has said, will say*): *"I am hungry."* → *She **says** she **is** hungry.*
2. The words are a **general truth** or still true: *"Water boils at 100 °C."* → *The teacher said water **boils** at 100 °C.*
3. The verb is already **past perfect**, or a modal like **would, could, should, might, ought to**.
**say or tell?** *say* has no person after it (*She said that…*, *She said to me…*). *tell* always has a person (*She **told me** that…*). ✗ *She said me*. ✗ *She told that*.

cards.title: Step by step: report a statement
cards.problem: Report: Hana said to me, "I am going to visit my aunt in Keren tomorrow."

steps.text: **Step 1: Reporting verb.** *said to me* → **told me** (tell + person).
**Step 2: Pronouns.** *I* → **she**; *my* → **her** (Hana is a woman).
**Step 3: Tense one step back.** *am going to* → **was going to**.
**Step 4: Time and place words.** *tomorrow* → **the next day**. (*Keren* is a name – no change.)
**Step 5: Put it together.** Hana told me (that) she was going to visit her aunt in Keren the next day.

cards.answer: Hana told me (that) she was going to visit her aunt in Keren the next day.

cards.title: Step by step: report a question
cards.problem: Report: He asked me, "Where did you buy this book yesterday?"

steps.text: **Step 1: Keep the question word.** *where*.
**Step 2: Statement order, no did.** *did you buy* → *you bought*.
**Step 3: Pronoun.** *you* (= me) → **I**.
**Step 4: Tense back.** past simple *bought* → past perfect **had bought**.
**Step 5: Time/place words.** *this* → **that**; *yesterday* → **the day before**.
**Step 6: Full stop, not a question mark.** He asked me where I had bought that book the day before.

cards.answer: He asked me where I had bought that book the day before.

body: In reported speech the tense moves back after a past reporting verb, pronouns and time words change, questions use if/whether or a wh-word with statement order, and requests or commands use asked/told + object + (not) to + verb.

cards.title: Step by step: Punctuation (2) – direct and reported speech
body: **Step 1:** Direct speech copies the exact words inside quotation marks: Selam said, "I am tired."
**Step 2:** Put a comma (or ? or !) before the closing quotation mark, and start the spoken words with a capital letter.
**Step 3:** Start a new line (paragraph) each time a new person speaks.
**Step 4:** Reported speech has no quotation marks: Selam said (that) she was tired – the tense moves one step back after a past reporting verb.
**Step 5:** A reported question is a statement, so it ends with a full stop, not a question mark: He asked me where I lived.
**Example:** Direct: "Where is the library?" asked Yonas. → Reported: Yonas asked where the library was. (no quotation marks, statement word order, full stop).

cards.title: Subject–verb agreement
rule: A singular subject takes a singular verb (*My friend **lives** here*); a plural subject takes a plural verb (*My friends **live** here*).
With **either ... or** and **neither ... nor**, the verb agrees with the **nearer** subject: *Neither the teacher nor the **students are** here.* / *Either the students or the **teacher is** here.*
**Together with, as well as, along with** do not change the subject: *The captain, together with his players, **is** coming.* **Each, every, everyone, nobody** take a singular verb.

steps.text: **Step 1: Find the time words.** *Listen!* and *right now* = happening now → present continuous (am/is/are + -ing).
**Step 2: Find the subject.** *The choir* = one group → singular → **is**.
**Step 3: Answer.** *The choir **is singing***.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: I ________ the main reason for his sudden decision to leave the scholarship program.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** *understand* is a **state verb** (a verb of thinking or feeling, not an action).

**Step 2:** State verbs do not take -ing: ✗ *am understanding*.

**Step 3:** Subject *I* → **understand** (no -s). So the answer is B.

**Tip:** State verbs (know, understand, like, want, believe, own) stay in the simple form: I understand, she knows.

**In Tigrinya:** 'Understand' (ምርዳእ) ሓደ ካብቶም ናይ ኣእምሮ ኩነታት ዝገልጹ ግሶች (state verbs) ስለ ዝኾነ፡ ቀጻሊ እዋን (continuous form) ክወስድ ኣይኽእልን እዩ። ኣብ ትግርኛ 'ይርድኣኒ ኣሎ' (ቀጻሊ ዝመስል) እንተበልና እኳ፡ ብእንግሊዘኛ ግን ወትሩ 'understand' (Option B) ጥራይ ኢና ክንጽሕፍ ዘለና።

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Samson as well as his two best friends _______ going to the library at the moment.
cards.why: When a subject is joined to another noun by phrases like 'as well as', 'along with', or 'together with', the verb agrees with the first subject. Here, 'Samson' is singular, so the verb must be singular ('is' or 'was'). The time marker 'at the moment' indicates the present continuous tense, making 'is' the correct choice.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The police ________ investigating the robbery that occurred near the national bank.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** *police* means the police officers – it is always plural in English.

**Step 2:** Plural subject → plural verb: **are** investigating.

**Step 3:** Do not be tricked: *police* has no -s, but it is still plural.

**Tip:** Find the real subject (cover phrases like "of the students" or "with his friends") and make the verb agree with it.

**In Tigrinya:** 'Police' (ፖሊስ) ዝብል ስም ክትርእዮ ከለኻ ናይ ነጸላ (singular) ይመስል እምበር፡ ብሰዋስው ግን ወትሩ ብዙሕ ቁጽሪ (plural) ተገይሩ ስለ ዝውሰድ ድሕሪኡ ዝመጽእ ግሲ 'are' (Option B) ክኸውን ኣለዎ።

cards.title: Step by step: "the number of" + singular verb
cards.problem: Complete: "Since the library was repaired, the number of visitors ____ (increase) a lot."

steps.text: **Step 1: Find the real subject.** *the number* (of visitors) – one number → singular.
**Step 2: Choose the tense.** *Since…* means from then until now → present perfect.
**Step 3: Put it together.** singular + present perfect → **has increased** (not *have*).
**Remember:** *the number of* + singular verb; *a number of* (= many) + plural verb.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Each of the candidates who applied for the engineering position ________ a written test.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** The subject is **Each** (each one) → singular.

**Step 2:** Ignore *of the candidates who applied…* – it only describes *each*.

**Step 3:** Singular → **has to take**.

**Tip:** Find the real subject (cover phrases like "of the students" or "with his friends") and make the verb agree with it.

**In Tigrinya:** እቲ ዋና ባእታ 'Each' (ነፍሲ ወከፍ) ስለ ዝኾነ፡ ብሰዋስው ወግዒ ነጸላ (singular) እዩ። ስለዚ ምስኡ ዝኸይድ ነጸላ ግሲ 'has to take' (Option A) ክኸውን ኣለዎ። 'candidates' (ሕጹያት) ዝብል ቃል ብዙሕ ስለ ዝኾነ 'have' ምምራጽ ጌጋ እዩ።

cards.title: Step by step: "one of" + singular verb
cards.problem: Complete: "One of the biggest problems for school leavers ____ the cost of university."

steps.text: **Step 1: Find the real subject.** *One* (of the problems) → singular.
**Step 2: Cover the middle words.** *One … ____ the cost* → *One **is***.
**Step 3: Do not match the verb with *problems*.** That word is inside the phrase *of the biggest problems*.

cards.title: Step by step: a group noun + singular verb
cards.problem: Complete: "The board of directors, although they had different ideas, ____ finally agreed on the budget."

steps.text: **Step 1: Find the real subject.** *The board* – one group → singular.
**Step 2: Cover the extra words.** *of directors* and *although they had different ideas* do not change the subject.
**Step 3: Choose the verb.** *The board **has** finally agreed.*

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Neither the regional program coordinator nor the senior researchers ________ present at the emergency project meeting yesterday.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** With *neither … nor*, the verb agrees with the subject **nearest** to it.

**Step 2:** The nearest subject is *the senior researchers* (plural).

**Step 3:** *yesterday* → past → **were**.

**Tip:** Find the real subject (cover phrases like "of the students" or "with his friends") and make the verb agree with it.

**In Tigrinya:** ምሉእ ሓሳብ ብ 'Neither... nor' ክእሰር ከሎ፡ እቲ ግሲ ምስቲ ናብኡ ዝቐረበ ባእታ ይሰማማዕ (Proximity Rule)። እቲ ዝቐረበ ባእታ 'the senior researchers' (ብዙሕ) ስለ ዝኾነን እቲ ግዜ ድማ 'yesterday' (ትማሊ) ስለ ዝኾነን፡ ቅኑዕ መልሲ 'were' (Option B) እዩ።

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The local police ________ currently searching the forest area for the prisoners who escaped from the regional jail.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** *police* is always plural.

**Step 2:** *currently* = now → present → **are** searching.

**Step 3:** *is* and *was* are singular; *were* is past.

**Tip:** Find the real subject (cover phrases like "of the students" or "with his friends") and make the verb agree with it.

**In Tigrinya:** 'Police' (ፖሊስ) ዝብል ስም ብቅርጹ ነጸላ ይመስል እምበር፡ ብሰዋስው ወግዒ ግን ወትሩ ብዙሕ ቁጽሪ (plural) እዩ። 'currently' (ኣብዚ እዋን) ዝብል ቃል ድማ ህልው እዋን ስለ ዝሕብር፡ ምስኡ ዝኸይድ ግሲ 'are' (Option B) እዩ።

cards.title: Parts of speech (2)
rule: An **adverb** describes a verb, adjective or another adverb (*She speaks **frankly***; *very* tall). Many adverbs = adjective + **-ly** (*happy → happily, easy → easily, late → lately* (= recently)). A **conjunction** joins (*and, because, although*). A **preposition** shows place, time or relation (*in, on, at, apart from*). An **interjection** shows feeling (*Oh! Wow! Ouch!*).

She sings beautiful.

**Step 2: Test the sentence.** "She sings beautiful." breaks this rule.

cards.title: Unit summary
body: Singular subjects take singular verbs and plural subjects plural verbs. With either/or and neither/nor the verb agrees with the nearer subject; phrases like together with do not change the subject. Adverbs describe verbs (often -ly); prepositions, conjunctions and interjections complete the parts of speech.

cards.title: Step by step: Parts of speech (2) – making the verb agree
body: **Step 1:** Find the subject (a noun or pronoun) and decide if it is singular or plural.
**Step 2:** A singular subject in the present simple takes verb + -s: "The girl reads." A plural subject takes the base verb: "The girls read."
**Step 3:** Ignore phrases between the subject and the verb: "The list of names is long."
**Step 4:** Words like everybody, someone, each, nobody are singular: "Everybody has arrived."
**Step 5:** With either…or / neither…nor the verb agrees with the nearer subject; with "together with / as well as" the verb agrees with the first subject.

**Example:** "The teacher, together with her students, (visit/visits) the museum." First subject = the teacher (singular) → visits. "Either the boys or their father (is/are) at home." Nearer subject = father → is.

cards.title: Mnemonic — "One subject, one -s"
body: the -s goes on the noun OR on the verb, not both (the dog barks / the dogs bark).

cards.title: Exam tip
body: Underline the subject and draw an arrow to the verb before choosing – it stops you being misled by the noun closest to the verb.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In "She answered the question correctly", what part of speech is "correctly"?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** "correctly" tells how she answered.

**Step 2:** Words that describe verbs are adverbs.

**Step 3:** So it is an adverb.

**Tip:** Ask what job the word does: names a thing → noun; describes a noun → adjective; tells how/when/where → adverb; shows place or time before a noun → preposition.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Choose the adjective form of "danger".
cards.why:
**Step 1:** The suffix -ous makes adjectives (famous, dangerous).

**Step 2:** "dangerously" is an adverb, "endanger" a verb, "dangers" a plural noun.

**Step 3:** So: dangerous.

**Tip:** Ask what job the word does: names a thing → noun; describes a noun → adjective; tells how/when/where → adverb; shows place or time before a noun → preposition.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In "We walked across the bridge", which word is a preposition?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** A preposition shows a relationship of place, direction or time between words.

**Step 2:** "across" shows direction in relation to "the bridge".

**Step 3:** The other words are a verb, a noun and a pronoun.

**Tip:** Ask what job the word does: names a thing → noun; describes a noun → adjective; tells how/when/where → adverb; shows place or time before a noun → preposition.

units.title: Energy
units.intro: Grammar: noun phrases with articles (a/an/the/zero), singular and plural nouns, and tag questions with be, do, have and will.

cards.title: Articles and noun phrases
rule: Use **a** before a consonant sound and **an** before a vowel sound with singular countable nouns mentioned for the first time: *a solar panel, an hour, a university*.
Use **the** when the noun is known or unique: *the sun, the energy we used, the Red Sea*.
Use **no article** (zero) with plural or uncountable nouns in general: *Energy is expensive. Trees give shade.*

examples.text: The sun gives us energy.
She bought an uniform.
Electricity is useful.
The electricity is useful for everyone in general.

cards.title: Step by step: few or little?
cards.problem: Complete: "The manager said no because ____ details were given." (too few / too little)

steps.text: **Step 1: Look at the noun.** *details* ends in -s, so it is a plural noun we can count.
**Step 2: Choose the word.** Countable → *few*. Uncountable → *little*.
**Step 3: Check the meaning.** The manager said no, so the meaning is negative: *too few* (not enough).

cards.title: Step by step: tricky plurals
cards.problem: Find the mistake: "The school board discussed several educational crisises."

steps.text: **Step 1: Find the plural noun.** *crisises*.
**Step 2: Remember the special plural.** Words ending in **-is** change to **-es**: *crisis → crises, analysis → analyses, thesis → theses*.
**Step 3: Correct it.** *several educational **crises***.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Although the construction project has been delayed, ________ progress has been made this week.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** *progress* is uncountable (no plural, no *a*).

**Step 2:** *a few, many, few* are only for countable nouns.

**Step 3:** *some* works with countable and uncountable nouns → **some progress**.

**Tip:** Can you count it? many / few / a few + plural. Can't count it? much / little / a little + singular. some works with both.

cards.title: Passive in continuous and perfect tenses
rule: **Present continuous passive:** am/is/are + **being** + past participle: *The road **is being repaired**.*
**Past continuous passive:** was/were + **being** + pp: *The hall **was being cleaned** when we arrived.*
**Present perfect passive:** has/have + **been** + pp: *The results **have been published**.* **Past perfect passive:** had + **been** + pp: *The tickets **had been sold** before we came.*

cards.title: Present perfect, present perfect continuous and past perfect
rule: **Present perfect** = *have/has + past participle*. Use it for a past action that is important **now**, or with no exact time: *I **have lost** my pen. She **has visited** Axum twice.*
Use **since** + a starting point (*since 2020, since Monday*) and **for** + a length of time (*for three years*): *We **have lived** here **for** ten years.*
**Present perfect continuous** = *have/has + been + -ing*. Use it for an action that started in the past and is **still going on**: *Aster **has been working** here **since** 2019.*
With a **finished time** (*yesterday, last week, ago, in 2015*) use the **past simple**, not the present perfect: *They **finished** the road three weeks ago.*
**Past perfect** = *had + past participle*: the **earlier** of two past actions: *When we arrived, the bus **had left**.*

**Step 2:** From the past until now → present perfect: **have lived**.

**Step 3:** *live / are living* are present only; *lived* is finished past.

**Tip:** since / for / already / yet / ever → present perfect (have + V3). Still going on + how long → have been + -ing. ago / yesterday → past simple.

**Step 3:** had been + past participle → **had been taken**.

**Tip:** Finished time (yesterday, ago, last…) → past simple. Long action interrupted → was/were + -ing. Earlier of two past actions → had + past participle.

units.intro: Grammar: talking about the future and conditional sentences type 1 (real/possible) and type 2 (unreal/imaginary).

cards.title: Conditionals type 1 and 2
rule: **Type 1 (real possibility):** *If + present simple, will + base verb.* *If the population **grows** fast, we **will need** more schools.*

**Type 2 (unreal or unlikely now/future):** *If + past simple, would + base verb.* *If I **had** more land, I **would grow** more food.* With be, use **were** for all persons in formal English: *If I **were** you, ...*
The if-clause can come second; then no comma: *We will need more schools if the population grows.*

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Look at those thick dark clouds hanging over the mountains! It ________ rain very soon.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** We can **see** the dark clouds now – that is evidence.

**Step 2:** A prediction from evidence → **is going to** rain.

**Step 3:** *will* is for a decision made now or a general prediction.

**Tip:** Evidence now → going to. Decision now → will. Timetable → present simple. Arrangement → present continuous.

**In Tigrinya:** ኣብቲ ከባቢ ንጹር ዝኾነ ናይ ዓይኒ መርትዖ (thick dark clouds - ጸሊም ደበና) ስለ ዘሎ፡ ንመጻኢ ትንቢት ክንገልጽ ከለና 'be going to' (Option B) ክንጥቀም ኣለና። መርትዖ ምስ ዘይህሉ ግን 'will' ምጥቃም ቅኑዕ ምኾነ።

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The public train to Djibouti ________ from the main station at exactly 7:30 AM tomorrow.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** A train leaving at a fixed time is a **timetable**.

**Step 2:** Timetables use the present simple even for the future → **departs**.

**Step 3:** Do not choose *will depart* just because you see *tomorrow*.

**Tip:** Evidence now → going to. Decision now → will. Timetable → present simple. Arrangement → present continuous.

**In Tigrinya:** ናይ ባቡር ወይ ነፋሪት መገሻ (timetable) ቀዋሚ ስርዓት ዘለዎ ስለ ዝኾነ፡ ንመጻኢ ግዜ ክንገልጽ ከለና ብ Present Simple 'departs' (Option B) ጥራይ ኢና ክንጽሕፍ ዘለና። 'tomorrow' ስለ ዘሎ 'will depart' ምምራጽ ጌጋ እዩ።

cards.title: Step by step: should have (regret)
cards.problem: Complete: "I failed the biology exam. I ____ (study) harder instead of wasting time on my phone."

steps.text: **Step 1: What happened?** I did **not** study hard, and now I am sorry.
**Step 2: Choose the modal.** A past regret (good idea, but I didn't do it) → **should have** + past participle.
**Step 3: Compare.** *must have studied* means "I am sure I studied" – the wrong meaning here.

cards.title: Step by step: mustn't or don't have to?
cards.problem: Complete: "Lab rule: you ____ enter the chemistry room without safety goggles."

steps.text: **Step 1: What does the rule say?** Entering without goggles is **not allowed**.
**Step 2: Choose.** not allowed → **must not (mustn't)**.
**Step 3: Compare.** *don't have to* = it is not necessary – the wrong meaning for a safety rule.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Aster has been studying and living in London for ten years, so she ________ speak English very fluently.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Ten years in London is strong evidence – we are sure about now.

**Step 2:** Sure about the present → **must** + base verb (*must speak*).

**Step 3:** *must have* is for the past and needs a past participle (*must have spoken*).

**Tip:** must = it is necessary / I am sure; mustn't = it is not allowed; don't have to = it is not necessary; should have + V3 = it was a good idea but you didn't; must have + V3 = I'm sure it happened.

**In Tigrinya:** እቲ ምሉእ ሓሳብ ኣብ ህልው እዋን ዘሎ ናይ ምርግጋጽ ስነ-ሞጎት (present logical deduction) የርእየና። 'ዓሰርተ ዓመት ኣብ ሎንዶን ስለ ዝነበረት' ዝብል መርትዖ ስለ ዘሎ፡ 'ብርግጽ ብጽቡቕ ትዛረብ እያ' ንምባል 'must' (Option A) ክንጥቀም ኣለና። 'must have' ግን ንሕሉፍ እዋን ጥራይ እዩ ዘገልግል።

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The soccer field is completely covered in puddles; it ________ heavily during the night.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** We see puddles now, so we are sure it rained in the night.

**Step 2:** Sure about the past → **must have** + past participle → **must have rained**.

**Step 3:** *should have rained* would mean it was a good idea for it to rain – that makes no sense.

**Tip:** must = it is necessary / I am sure; mustn't = it is not allowed; don't have to = it is not necessary; should have + V3 = it was a good idea but you didn't; must have + V3 = I'm sure it happened.

**In Tigrinya:** 'እቲ ናይ ኲዕሶ እግሪ ሜዳ ብማይ ተሸፊኑ ኣሎ' ዝብል ናይ ዓይኒ መርትዖ ስለ ዘለና፡ 'ትማሊ ምሸት ብርግጽ ዓቢ ዝናብ ዘኒቡ ክኸውን ኣለዎ' (past logical deduction) ንምባል 'must have rained' (Option B) ክንመርጽ ኣለና። 'should have' ግን ጣዕሳ ጥራይ እዩ ዝገልጽ።

cards.title: Conditional type 3
rule: **Form:** *If + past perfect, would have + past participle.* *If she **had studied**, she **would have passed**.*

**Meaning:** an imaginary past: the condition did **not** happen, so the result did not happen either. It is often used for regrets: *If I **had known** about my fear of heights, I **wouldn’t have climbed** the tower.*
Could have / might have can replace would have: *If we had left earlier, we **might have caught** the bus.*
